# Air Vent An air vent is the standard ventilation device found in every room that needs to be filled with a breathable atmosphere. Its primary purpose is to transfer gases into the surrounding atmosphere until the set pressure is reached.
An air vent requires [textlink="power" link="Power"] from a nearby [textlink="LV cable" link="VoltageNetworks"] to operate.
An air vent can be welded shut with any welding tool to stop it from operating.
## Default Operation By default, an air vent simply releases gas into the surrounding atmosphere until it reaches [color=orange][protodata="GasVentPump" comp="GasVentPump" member="DefaultExternalBound"/] kPa[/color].
The vent's rate depends on the difference between twice the pressure of the connected [textlink="pipe network" link="PipeNetworks"] and the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere. As a formula:
[italic]Rate = 2 × pipe network pressure - surrounding atmosphere pressure[/italic]
For example, this means that the vent cannot pump the atmosphere to 101.3 kPa if the gas pressure inside the vent itself falls below half that value.
## Pressure Lockout Air vents enter [color=red]pressure lockout[/color] when the surrounding atmosphere's pressure is below [color=orange][protodata="GasVentPump" comp="GasVentPump" member="UnderPressureLockoutThreshold"/] kPa[/color]. This prevents useful gases from being wasted into space when a room is not airtight. The vent's indicators will turn [color=yellow]yellow[/color] to show this state.
This can be [color=green]overridden[/color] by right-clicking the vent and selecting 'Release pressure lock out', or by setting the connected [textlink="air alarm" link="AirAlarms"] to Fill mode.
It is important to remember that vents in [color=red]pressure lockout[/color] still release gas very slowly. The amount released depends on the current pressure of the pipe network they are connected to.
## Settings When [textlink="linked" link="Networking"] to an [textlink="air alarm" link="AirAlarms"], air vents gain additional options.
Air vents have two "vent direction" options: Releasing and Siphoning. - Releasing simply releases gases from the connected pipe network into the atmosphere. - Siphoning draws air from the atmosphere into the connected pipe network. The vent's indicators will turn [color=red]red[/color] to show this change.
## Pressure Bounds Air vents have a system of pressure bounds that controls the pressure to which a vent will fill the atmosphere or draw gas from the connected pipe network. These bounds apply in both Releasing and Siphoning modes.
The "PressureBound" setting has four options: - ExternalBound makes the vent obey the pressure limit in the External bound field. - InternalBound makes the vent obey the pressure limit in the Internal bound field. - Both makes the vent obey both the External and Internal bound limits. - NoBound disables the limits.
When the vent is in Releasing mode: - If External bound is set to 101.3 kPa, the vent will not raise the atmosphere above 101.3 kPa. - If Internal bound is set to 50 kPa, the vent will not take gas from the connected pipe if its pressure is below 50 kPa.
When the vent is in Siphoning mode: - If External bound is set to 101.3 kPa, the vent will siphon gases until the atmosphere reaches 101.3 kPa. - If Internal bound is set to 50 kPa, the vent will not push gases into the pipe network if its pressure is above 50 kPa.
If PressureBounds are still confusing, here is a simple way to think about them: - External bound is the upper limit for the surrounding atmosphere. "I will not pump the surrounding atmosphere above this pressure or take gas from it below this pressure." - Internal bound is the lower limit for the connected pipe network. "I will not take gas from a source below this pressure or push air into the pipe network above this pressure." - The "Pressure bound" settings simply determine which limits to obey and which to ignore.
